name: Tzu-Hsiang (Sean) Lin
meta_description: Sean Lin — robotics, safe control, perception, and mechanical engineering at the University of Michigan.
about: I am a graduate student in Mechanical Engineering (Robotics) at the [University of Michigan](https://umich.edu/) in the USA. I graduated from [University of Nottingham](https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/) in the UK with the first honour class degree in Mechanical Engineering. My interests span **Safe Planning and Control, Trajectory Optimization, SLAM and Multi-robot System for Aerial Robotics**.

At Michigan, research spans multi-agent aerial systems and safe control in the [Distributed Autonomous System and Control (DASC) Lab](https://dasc-lab.github.io/), pneumatic micro-actuation in the [Zoetic Robotics Lab](https://www.zoeticrobotics.com/), and magnetic microrobot control in the [SAM Lab](https://samlab.robotics.umich.edu/). Current work includes a 3D Gaussian Splatting aerial simulator connecting scene reconstruction, visual simulation, and future sim-to-real deployment.

Previously, I worked in [Advanced Robotics Laboratory](https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/research/groups/advanced-manufacturing-technology-research-group/research/advanced-robotics.aspx) at the University of Nottingham working on the Underwater Bio-inspired Soft Robotics. This summer, I worked as a Product Design Engineering Intern at [Apple](https://www.apple.com/). I have also worked in the aerospace industry for eVTOL development at [Bellwether Industries](https://www.bellwether-industries.com/). The long-term goal is to develop complete robotic platforms that bring hardware design and autonomy together.
personal_about: Outside research and engineering, I enjoy learning through sport, travel, and hands-on hobbies. I love all kinds of water sports as well as Tennis and Golf

projects.name: SEAMLiS
projects.cover_alt: SEAMLiS comparison results above the multi-robot autonomy system architecture.
projects.summary: Perception-aware safety for multi-robot exploration, from simulation to Crazyflie hardware.
projects.alt: SEAMLiS architecture connecting planning, perception, attitude control and positional control.
projects.caption: SEAMLiS team framework: planning, perception and safety control.
paragraphs: Limited sensing can leave a robot moving toward an obstacle while its sensor looks elsewhere. The team developed a safety framework for exploration under these perception constraints.
Supported deployment of the system on Crazyflie platforms, integrated planning, control and motion capture through ROS interfaces and coordinate transformations, and conducted hardware experiments.
Work focused on the interface between the team’s planning and safety modules and physical flight. Investigated controller instability, estimation error, communication latency and model mismatch.
Single-robot and multi-agent hardware experiments were conducted in GPS-denied environments. The supplied material does not establish a quantitative performance comparison for the deployment work.
[Read the SEAMLiS preprint on arXiv ↗](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09959)
projects.card_summary: Perception-aware safety for multi-robot aerial exploration under limited sensing. Work includes Crazyflie deployment, ROS integration of planning, control and motion capture, and hardware experiments investigating estimation error, delay and controller behavior.

projects.name: Toward Safe Sim-to-Real Visual Control Using a 3DGS Aerial Simulator
projects.summary: Building a photorealistic simulation pipeline for visual policies and aerial robot deployment.
projects.alt: 3DGS aerial-simulator project outline with reconstruction, visual-policy training and sim-to-real stages.
projects.caption: Project outline and related work. Visual-policy training, sim-to-real and safety-filter integration are development goals.

gallery.alt: Aerial robot in the DASC Lab flight-testing space.
gallery.caption: Aerial platform in the laboratory flight-testing environment.

paragraphs: Vision policies need useful training observations and a credible path to hardware. This project combines a reconstructed laboratory appearance with aerial-robot dynamics.
Developing the simulator and the training/deployment pipeline, investigating how scene reconstruction, camera observations and robot dynamics fit together.
The planned pipeline links 3DGS scene appearance, collision geometry, synchronized robot/camera poses and policy training. Training-method selection and hardware transfer remain development work.
The pipeline is being established. Completed visual-policy training, faster deployment and successful zero-shot transfer are not claimed.
projects.card_summary: Developing a photorealistic aerial simulation pipeline using 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct the laboratory environment. The project connects scene appearance with collision geometry and camera rendering, with visual-policy training and future sim-to-real deployment as development goals.

projects.name: TEG-SLAM
projects.summary: Temporal evidence and memory-aware pose estimation in a 3D Gaussian SLAM pipeline.
projects.alt: TEG-SLAM rendering, depth, uncertainty and reconstruction-error analysis.
projects.caption: TEG-SLAM qualitative analysis of rendered RGB, metric depth, uncertainty and reconstruction error.
paragraphs: Work on TEG-SLAM focuses on extending Wild-GS SLAM with temporal information to improve camera trajectory estimation and scene reconstruction. This 3D Gaussian SLAM project includes a memory-aware pose-estimation module that modifies Lie-group state updates and integrates temporal features within the optimization pipeline.

Rather than processing each observation independently, the pipeline incorporates information across successive frames into tracking and mapping. Temporal evidence supports pose estimation and helps maintain a more consistent Gaussian representation of the scene.
The project results reported in the resume include an 18% reduction in absolute trajectory error (ATE) and 2–5% improvements in PSNR and SSIM over the baseline.
projects.card_summary: Work on TEG-SLAM extends Wild-GS SLAM with temporal information to improve trajectory estimation and scene reconstruction. The project includes memory-aware pose estimation, Lie-group state updates and temporal feature integration within a 3D Gaussian SLAM optimization pipeline.

projects.name: 5-DoF Robotics Arm Perception and Control
projects.summary: RGB-D block detection, camera calibration and kinematics for semi-autonomous pick-and-place.
projects.alt: Detected colored blocks and calibrated markers in the robot-arm workspace.
projects.caption: Block-detection view from the 5-DoF arm project.
paragraphs: This project connects computer vision with the motion of a 5-DoF robotic arm for semi-autonomous pick-and-place. An Intel RealSense RGB-D camera observes colored blocks in the workspace, while a Python pipeline combines visual detections, coordinate transformations and kinematic reasoning to identify reachable targets.

Intrinsic camera calibration relates image measurements to camera geometry, and extrinsic calibration aligns the camera with the robot coordinate frame. This alignment allows detected block locations to be interpreted in the same coordinate system used to command the arm.

OpenCV-based block detection identifies objects in the camera view. Product-of-exponentials kinematics describes the relationship between the arm’s joint configuration and end-effector pose, connecting the perception pipeline with physical manipulation.
The implementation brings together sensing, calibration and arm execution in a single workflow. The resume reports an average positional error of 1.9% for the project.
projects.card_summary: Integrated RGB-D perception, camera calibration and kinematic reasoning for a 5-DoF robotic arm. OpenCV-based block detection and calibrated coordinate transformations connect visual observations with semi-autonomous pick-and-place motion.

projects.name: Mobile Robot Autonomy System
projects.summary: Embedded mapping, particle-filter localization, A* planning and feedback control.
projects.alt: Mobile robot hardware alongside its occupancy-grid map in RViz.
projects.caption: Mobile robot platform and occupancy-grid mapping in RViz.
paragraphs: This project integrates perception, localization, planning and feedback control on a differential-drive mobile robot. A C++ and ROS2 environment running on a Raspberry Pi connects 2D LiDAR, an IMU and wheel encoders to support navigation with noisy sensor measurements.

Occupancy-grid mapping represents free space and obstacles from LiDAR measurements, using Bresenham’s algorithm to trace sensor rays through the grid. Monte Carlo localization maintains a set of possible robot poses and updates their likelihood as motion and sensor observations become available.

A* planning searches the map for a route to a target, while cascade PID controllers translate motion commands into wheel-level behavior. Together, these components connect a map and pose estimate with executable robot motion.

Runtime analysis examined whether particle-filter localization could run within the embedded system’s computation budget. The resume reports real-time localization at 10 Hz with up to thousands of particles, linking algorithm design with practical onboard performance.
projects.card_summary: Built an embedded autonomy stack connecting perception, localization, planning and feedback control. The differential-drive platform combines occupancy-grid mapping, Monte Carlo Localization, A* planning and PID control using LiDAR, IMU and wheel-encoder data.

paragraphs: This collaborative research explores pneumatically actuated, bio-inspired micro aerial robots. The research connects nonlinear actuator models with instrumentation and experimental measurements.

Developed experimental instrumentation and data-acquisition workflows for pneumatically actuated aerial robots, including design, simulation and mathematical modeling. Developed physics-based and semi-empirical models of nonlinear pneumatic actuator behavior and compared model predictions with experimental measurements.

projects.name: Centrifugal Clutch
projects.summary: A speed-dependent clutch combining mechanical analysis, CAD and manufacturing design.
projects.alt: Annotated centrifugal-clutch assembly and component layout.
projects.caption: Annotated centrifugal-clutch assembly and component layout.

gallery.alt: Manufactured centrifugal-clutch prototype on a workbench.
gallery.caption: Manufactured centrifugal-clutch prototype.

gallery.alt: Early centrifugal-clutch mechanism sketches and design notes.
gallery.caption: Early mechanism concepts and design notes.

paragraphs: This group design-and-make project developed a centrifugal clutch to transfer rotational power from a motor to a generator once the motor reaches a chosen engagement speed. The design balances centrifugal force, spring restraint and frictional contact to connect the rotating input with the output drum.

The team design uses twin leading shoes, dowel pins, an adjustable spring arrangement and a drive plate. Nylon 12 shoes carry Permali friction linings that contact an aluminum drum when centrifugal force exceeds the spring restraint.

Design requirements included engagement around 1,200 rpm and a minimum transmitted torque of 0.5 N·m at 2,300 rpm. Calculations informed spring stiffness, shoe geometry and mass, shaft sizing, material selection and component fits.

The critical design review combined annotated CAD, mechanical calculations, manufacturing considerations and an iterative design process. These are team design targets and analysis documented in the report, rather than claimed measured test results.
projects.card_summary: A team design-and-make project developing a centrifugal clutch for speed-dependent power transmission. Annotated CAD and mechanical calculations connect spring restraint, shoe geometry, frictional contact and material selection with engagement-speed and torque requirements.

projects.name: Uncertainty-Aware Visual Planning with DINO World Models
projects.alt: Architecture for uncertainty-aware visual planning with ensemble DINO world models and risk-aware MPPI.
projects.caption: Proposed offline world-model training and online risk-aware visual-planning pipeline.
projects.summary: Work in progress: uncertainty-aware visual planning with ensemble latent world models and risk-aware MPPI.
paragraphs: This work-in-progress project investigates uncertainty-aware visual planning for aerial robots using an ensemble of latent world models and risk-aware Model Predictive Path Integral control.
The proposed offline pipeline uses RGB observations and actions, a frozen DINOv2 encoder, and an ensemble of vision-transformer world models trained to predict the next latent observation.

During online planning, candidate action sequences are rolled out through the ensemble. Model disagreement provides an uncertainty estimate, while the risk-aware MPPI objective considers both goal error and predicted uncertainty when selecting an action.
The diagram presents the intended architecture and expected benefits. Implementation, evaluation, and collision-reduction results are still in progress and are not claimed as completed outcomes.
projects.card_summary: Work in progress on an uncertainty-aware visual-planning pipeline that combines frozen DINOv2 features, ensemble latent world models, and risk-aware MPPI for aerial-robot navigation.
projects.affiliation: University of Michigan · Work in progress

projects.name: Crazyflie Model Predictive Control for Trajectory Tracking
projects.alt: Crazyflie trajectory-tracking experiment in a robotics laboratory.
projects.caption: Crazyflie control and trajectory-tracking experiment.

gallery.caption: Crazyflie trajectory-tracking test in the laboratory.

projects.summary: Implementing nonlinear MPC for Crazyflie trajectory tracking with ROS 2, Gazebo, and Acados.
paragraphs: This project implements a nonlinear Model Predictive Controller for Crazyflie trajectory tracking as part of the University of Michigan AE 740 Online Learning for Control Lab 04 exercises.

The controller uses a simplified quadrotor model with a nine-dimensional state and four control inputs. The finite-horizon optimization penalizes state-tracking error and control effort while enforcing system dynamics and state and input constraints.

The implementation connects a ROS 2 control node, an Acados optimization problem, and Crazyflie software-in-the-loop simulation in Gazebo, with the workflow designed to support takeoff and circular-trajectory demonstrations.

The [official AE 740 Lab 04 exercise](https://um-iral.github.io/ae-740-website/labs/lab-04/exercises/) provides the problem formulation and implementation requirements. No quantitative tracking-performance claim is made from the supplied video.
projects.card_summary: Nonlinear MPC implementation for Crazyflie trajectory tracking using ROS 2, Gazebo, Acados, and a simplified quadrotor model, based on the University of Michigan AE 740 Lab 04 workflow.
